OLD MUSIC, NEW TIMES
Zhangsun Shaoyuan and the Ritual Music of the Northern Zhou
NOA HEGESH*
With the spread and flourishing of non-Han musical cultures, instruments, and performances in China’s Period of Division (220–589 CE), some musical customs 
within the northern ruling courts persisted in the vein of their Han predecessors. 
Courtiers and officials drew upon canonical texts as they engaged in discussions 
about musical execution, at times offering their own innovative interpretations. 
This article focuses on one such intense exchange between two members of the 
newly established Northern Zhou (557–581 CE). The official Zhangsun Shaoyuan 
(506–565) and Pei Zheng (d. 590), then a captive official from the state of Liang, 
debated over the number and organization of suspended bells in the ritual music 
performances of the dynasty. I argue that these debates extended far beyond the 
mere selection of pieces or ensembles; experts reflected the political ideologies 
they sought to advance through the use of music theory. In this case, the proposition 
involved an interpretative model of the old Zhou dynasty ritual music, versus the 
former musical model of the Han, with its embedded cosmological and political 
views, especially regarding the position of the emperor.
KEYWORDS: Ritual music, Period of Division, pitch standards, politics, bells
ABBREVIATIONS
LSCQ Lüshi Chunqiu 呂氏春秋
INTRODUCTION

under its second ruling emperor, it became a priority to establish ritual music for 
the dynasty to signal legitimacy and future stability. To this end, Emperor Ming 
明 (r. 557–560) ordered a debate between two music experts over the number of

bells to be used in ritual music.1 At the surface level, this debate was a rhetorical contest 
of music theory between literati who wished to win the emperor’s favor. A closer look, 
however, reveals that the debate laid out two competing political models that reflect 
two very different approaches regarding the role of emperor. In this article I argue 
that music theory served as the foundation on which to construct political arguments 
in various ways. In this case, the cosmological-political model of the Han dynasty was 
pitted against the perceived ideology of a ruler-centered and non-cosmological model of 
the ancient Zhou dynasty. These considerations motivated literati even in practical 
matters such as the bell arrangement of the new dynastic ritual music.
Two central issues lay at the core of this debate. The first was a dispute over the 
application of music theory in new imperial ritual music performance throughout 
the year, concealed within a discussion over the use of a dalü 大呂 (great regulator) 
bell. The second was a dispute over the correct source of knowledge. The author of 
the text in which this debate is recounted, and its protagonist Zhangsun Shaoyuan 
長孫紹遠 (506–565), aimed to discredit the Lüshi Chunqiu 呂氏春秋 (Spring and 
Autumn Annals of Master Lü, hereafter LSCQ) as an authoritative source on 
cosmic synchrony, especially with respect to one of its main topics: sound. Their 
larger goal was to exalt the Zhouli 周禮 (Rituals of Zhou) as the ultimate guide, 
befitting the new Zhou dynasty.
The first section of this article introduces the main figures involved in the debate, 
detailing their backgrounds to convey their intellectual and personal stakes in the 
dispute. The second section sets the mise-en-scène by recounting the discovery of 
the huangzhong 黃鐘 (yellow bell) and addressing the question of legitimacy for 
the newly established Northern Zhou dynasty. The third section delves into the 
debate, analyzing it through the lenses of music theory and ideological implications.
THE ADVERSARIES
Both music experts in this debate were accomplished literati with exceptional abilities. Although their biographies are somewhat brief, they are rich enough to allow 
the reader to envision fully developed characters. The characters and backgrounds 
of these men help us better understand the significance of the debate and appreciate 
the intellectual and political prowess of two officials, who seem to be bickering over 
the use of a single bell with great fervor.
Zhangsun Shaoyuan, styled Shi 師, was a native of Luoyang. He hailed from a 
strong family that served the Northern Wei.2 Ethnically, he probably belonged to 
the Tuoba Zhangsun family of Dai 代 State (today in Inner Mongolia).3 He 
became a high official and served the Northern Wei (386–534), Western Wei

(535–557), and Northern Zhou under various titles, the highest of which was Grand 
Minister of Music (da siyue 大司樂).
Zhangsun’s biographer admired him.4 He opens the biography with a characterization of him as a magnanimous and tolerant figure and emphasizes that he was 
appointed Horse Pasturage Official of Shou Chun 壽春 at only thirteen years of 
age.5 When a Secretary at the Pasturage office named Wang Shi 王碩 heard of 
Zhangsun Shaoyuan’s impressive memorization skills, he asked to examine the 
young man on the “Yue ling” 月令 (Monthly Ordinances) chapter in the Liji 禮記 
(Book of Rites). The biographer’s choice of “Yue ling,” which lays out a correlative 
ritual scheme for the activities to be held in each month, must have been deliberate, 
as it foretells Zhangsun’s later roles in the Department of Rites and as Grand Minister of Music, an office that required the correct and timely execution of ritual 
music. We are told that “Shaoyuan read several pages, went over them once, and 
recited them like a stream.”6
Zhangsun Shaoyuan made his name as a can junshi 參軍事 (adjutant) in the Situ 
fu 司徒府 (Ministry of Education). After the pacification of the Hedong Shu Xue 河 
東蜀薛 clan,7 he assumed the title Dong E xian bo 東阿縣伯 (District Earl of Dong 
E).8 When the Northern Wei collapsed in 534, he fled Luoyang westwards with 
Emperor Xiaowu 孝武 (r. 532–535) and continued his diligent and exceptional 
service, for which he was rewarded with the title Wen’an xianzi 文安縣子 (District 
Viscount of Wen’an). After Yuwen Tai 宇文泰 poisoned Emperor Xiaowu and 
enthroned Yuan Baoju 元寶炬 as Emperor Wen of Wei (Wei Wendi 魏文帝, 
r. 535–551), Zhangsun Shaoyuan served the new emperor. He advanced to the position of taichang qing 太常卿 (Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices), 
and from there to the influential position of zhongshu ling 中書令 (Secretariat Director), inheriting his father’s title. He was later demoted to the title of gong 公 (Duke) 
and transferred to Fengyi 馮翊 commandery.
9 In 555, during the brief reign of 
Emperor Gong (Gongdi 恭帝, r. 553–556), Zhangsun Shaoyuan was again promoted, this time to the title of lu shangshu shi 錄尚書事 (Overseer of the Department 
of State Affairs). Yuwen Tai, the real power behind the emperor, often told his ministers, “When Duke Zhangsun is in charge, the people do not glance back with 
worry. Xiao [He] and Kou [Xun] are hardly worth mentioning. His dignified

presence and demeanor are sufficient to make him an exemplar for our times.”
10
When Emperor Gong of the Western Wei implemented the Six Offices system in 
556, just one year before the rise of the Northern Zhou, Zhangsun Shaoyuan 
received the high title of da siyue 大司樂. A year later, Emperor Xiaomin 孝閔 
(r. 557) of Zhou also conferred on him the title of Duke of Shang Dang.
Zhangsun’s adversary in the debate was Pei Zheng 裴正 (d. 590), styled Debiao 德 
表.
11 Like Zhangsun, he came from a prominent family, and he is described by his 
biographer in similar words: “Bright and clever from a young age, with keen intellect, extensive knowledge, and a sharp understanding of political affairs, he was 
praised by his contemporaries.”12 He was a high official at the court of the Liang 
dynasty and a descendent of Emperor Wu (Wudi 武帝, r. 420–422), founder of 
the Liu-Song 劉宋 dynasty (420–479).
At the age of fifteen, Pei was appointed as an administrator in the Law Section of 
the manor of the Prince of Shaoling (Bi Shaoling wangfu facao canjun shi 辟邵陵王府 
法曹參軍事). From then on, he moved up the ranks. During the rebellion of the northern General Hou Jing 後景 (d. 552), he used his military expertise to defend the Liang 
and followed the famous General Wang Lin 王琳 to battle. His military achievements 
earned him the title Marquess of Yiling (Yiling hou 夷陵侯). 13 He also received the 
honorific office of Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate (Huangmen shilang 黃門 
侍郎) when he followed Wang Lin once more to assist in the defeat of the emperor’s 
younger brother, Xiao Ji 蕭紀, a pretender to the throne.14 Although his biographies 
list additional titles bestowed upon him over the years, it is with this title that he is 
introduced in the anecdote analyzed in this article.
Pei Zheng was one of thousands of prisoners taken in 554, when the Western Wei 
attacked Jiangling 江陵, then the capital of the Liang.15 His biography details his 
capture by Xiao Cha 蕭察, the Liang prince and future puppet emperor of the 
Later Liang (Hou Liang 後梁, 555–587) who was allied to the Western Wei. Xiao 
Cha persuaded Pei Zheng to defect by promising status if he joined or death if he 
refused. Pei was then brought to the city walls and ordered to mislead Emperor Yuan 
by calling out that commander Wang Sengbian 王僧辯 had already declared himself 
emperor and that Wang Lin was weak and could not come to their aid. Instead, Pei 
Zheng called out to the people within the walls, “Large reinforcement is on the way. 
Embolden yourselves, each of you! I was captured while on a secret envoy [to warn

Wei capital, as his prisoner.
This event won Pei Zheng the admiration of Yuwen Tai, who by then was the ruler 
of the Western Wei (posthumously Emperor Wen 文, r. 560–578), and who 
appointed him Gentleman Cavalier Attendant (Yuanwai sanqi shilang 員外散騎 
侍郎)
17 and entrusted him, along with the literatus Lu Bian 盧辯, to establish the 
Six Ministries (liuguan 六官) in accordance with the Zhouli 周禮 (Rituals of 
Zhou), by selecting officials of all ranks, compiling ritual protocols concerning carriages, clothing, and utensils for the dynasties, and more.18 Thus, by the time he is 
introduced in the debate, Pei Zheng was a valued official in the Wei and Zhou 
courts. Following the debate, under Yuwen Yong 宇文邕 (posthumously Emperor 
Wu, r. 561–578), Pei took part in compiling the Zhou penal code (Zhoulü 周律). He 
continued as a high-ranking official under the Sui and later took part in compiling its 
legal code as well.
A strange, personal comment in the middle of the biography mentions that Pei had 
an affinity for drinking and that, as Vice Minister of Law (Shaosi jian 少司憲), “he 
could drink alcohol, consuming up to several dou 斗 without getting drunk. Case 
files piled up voluminously, but he decided them like a flowing stream, applying the 
law impartially and equitably without any injustice or abuse.”19 He allowed prisoners visitation rights with their wives and children. His fairness was so revered that 
those sentenced to execution went willingly and without resentment.
The biography only briefly mentions Pei’s musical expertise and references the 
debate with Zhangsun Shaoyuan with no details: “He also excelled in tuning (acoustics) and once discussed ritual music with Zhangsun Shaoyuan. Their dialogue is 
recorded in the ‘Treatise on Tuning Standards.’”20 The rest of Pei Zheng’s biography 
concerns his later roles under the Sui. He assisted in compiling the Sui legal code as 
head advisor and enjoyed a strong reputation as one willing to criticize those in 
power, no matter the cost. The last anecdote in the biography describes how he reprimanded the notorious craftsman-turned-official Yun Dingxing 雲定興 for ruining 
the reputation of the Sui crown prince Yang Yong 楊勇 (d. 604) by frequently inviting him to visit his concubines, offering him rare and valuable gifts, and staging 
musical performances to flatter and bribe him.21 For venturing this criticism, Pei

ZHANGSUN SHAOYUAN AND THE RITUAL MUSIC OF THE NORTHERN ZHOU 153

Zheng was sent away from the capital without his wife and children to govern 
Xiangzhou 襄州 (in modern Hubei province). When the crown prince was 
deposed in 600, Emperor Wen of Sui lamented, “If Pei Zheng and Liu Xingben 劉 
行本 were still here, it may not have come to this.”
22 Pei composed a text titled 
Chengsheng shilu 承聖實錄 (Vertitable Records of the Chengsheng Era) in ten 
scrolls.23 He died when he was eighty-nine.
SETTING THE STAGE
A symbolic bestowal of political and cosmic legitimacy opens the anecdote: 
At first, when Shaoyuan was appointed Minister of Ceremonials, he widely recruited 
artisans to build musical instruments. Only the huangzhong (yellow bell) was out of 
tune, and he always regretted it.24 Once, he passed by the Buddhist temple of Prefectural Governor Han and heard a Duo bell ringing from atop the third floor of the 
pagoda. Its tone was elegant and conformed to the tuning of the gong scale. Therefore, 
he fetched it (the bell) and played along with it. Only then could harmony be 
achieved.25
Huangzhong, the most important pitch-standard in the traditional musical system, 
was used to set the pitch of other instruments. Zhangsun Shaoyuan recognized the 
sound issued from a Buddhist pagoda as that lost fundamental, rendering all previous attempts by the Wei dynasty obsolete.26 With the true huangzhong in his possession, he could accurately tune the instruments he commissioned, as Minister of 
Ceremonials, for the dynastic rituals.
This symbolic literary gesture weaves the Western Wei and Northern Zhou Buddhist tradition together with one of the main threads of Han culture the music 
system. The shift in the origin of the correct huangzhong pitch to a Buddhist 
locus also signals the legitimacy of the Zhou as a ruling dynasty: “Harmony” is 
achieved both musically and politically.
The fortuitous occasion of the huangzhong sounding just as Zhangsun Shaoyuan 
passed by the pagoda is likely a rhetorical exercise in myth creation.27 A tradition of 
legitimacy confirmed by possession of the correct huangzhong pitch had long 
existed. It symbolized that the Mandate of Heaven had shifted to new hands –

especially, in this case, when the pitch was emitted from a Buddhist pagoda.28 A 
well-tuned huangzhong and its accompanying scale were used not only in cosmological debates concerning the calendar but also in ritual musical performances.29
Thus the anecdote emphasizes that correct ritual music must use the agreed-upon 
pitch standards. It is for this purpose that Zhangsun was gathering craftsmen to 
build musical instruments.
The symbolic meaning of this episode is underscored when, after the debate, 
Zhangsun Shaoyuan denominates the Northern Zhou the true and legitimate 
ruling house in a petition to the emperor: 
Whereupon he reported to Emperor Ming and said, “When the Wei dynasty came to 
establish their residence in the Qin and Yong provinces, although they followed 
ancient precedents in their musical pieces, so that huangzhong was the ruler – the 
correct position of the Son of Heaven – when they attempted to create it [a proper 
huangzhong], throughout the years it was not achieved.30 It was then that I knew 
the water phase [of the Northern Wei] neared its end and the wood phase [of the 
Northern Zhou] had begun.
The Mandate of Heaven has found its receiver, and the music of the [ancestral] 
spirits has descended. This was probably due only to the blessing and assistance of 
Heaven and earth and the ancestral shrine [of the Northern Zhou] being moved, 
such that they [the ancestors] sent down an object to harmonize with the spirits.31
Your [claim to the] throne will continue [to pass down] for ten thousand 
generations.”32
The term lingyue 靈樂 (music of the spirits) refers to ritual music practices handed 
down from the Han dynasty to the Cao Wei and Jin dynasties.33 Zhangsun suggests 
that the discovery of the bell indicates that the emperor, a Tabgatch ruler, received 
the spirits’ blessing – and their music – in keeping with Han customs. He explains

that previous Wei rulers failed to gain the blessing of the ancestors, and the sign was 
their inability to secure a properly tuned huangzhong. Only once the ancestral spirits 
were moved did they send the pagoda bell to signal their approval and declare that 
the mandate had passed to the new Zhou dynasty.
34 In this way, Zhangsun declares 
his loyalty to Emperor Ming, who, in return, promotes him and accepts the grave 
responsibility he has indicated: 
The edict said: “My humble self, what virtue do I possess to deserve this? It is owed to 
the blessings of Heaven and earth and that of the ancestors. It is also owed to your 
accurate perception.” Soon thereafter, Zhangsun Shaoyuan was transferred to the position of Ordinary Grand Master in the Department of Rites.35
The discovery of the correctly pitched huangzhong, finally bestowed by the ancestors, sets the stage for affirming the Zhou as a legitimate dynasty governed by a 
righteous ruler.
36 Having recounted how the emperor’s legitimacy is established, 
the author closes the scene and shifts to a new one concerning the practicalities of 
ritual music.
THE ORDER OF THINGS
In his new position, Zhangsun Shaoyuan sought to establish the dynastic ritual

CONCLUSION
The debate between Zhangsun Shaoyuan and Pei Zheng reveals how a significant 
ideological divergence could be reflected in musical practices and how music theory 
could be utilized to manifest a chosen political model. Changes in the organization 
of bells may have been unnoticeable to an audience with untrained ears or lacking 
theoretical knowledge, but the resulting performative act, which included the selection of the correct key for performance and its associated ritual, music, songs, and 
dances – all these were quite noticeable.
Methodologically, both experts focused on textual authority to anchor their ideological as well as their technical arguments. Zhangsun Shaoyuan repeatedly emphasized the sovereignty of the ruler as opposed to any cosmological consideration 
regarding the distribution of sounds. In his view, the ruler shaped the soundscape 
rather than being governed by it. This position allowed Zhangsun to propose a 
novel idea anchored in an old text. The use of eight bells to construct two fundamental scales (and several modes) through the use of common tones, along with 
the option of suspending a bell to symbolize the ruler and leaving it silent yet powerful, was a creative and novel idea.
Pei Zheng, while also giving the ruler his rightful position by retaining huangzhong as the fundamental pitch standard, relied on cosmological models in which 
the emperor is “an indispensable mediator” between Heaven and earth, macrocosm 
and microcosm.95 The sonic model that accompanied this conceptualization functioned only as part of a resonating system that tied sound to seasonal changes, the 
months and days of the year, qi and the important astronomical events. All these 
together dictated the appropriate scale for ritual and, in this system, the huangzhong 
scale belongs to the winter solstice. The idea of keeping the pitch as an external 
addition to a scale and not use it simply did not exist. Moreover, doing so would 
distort the entire model.
This case study exemplifies ways that we can extract information from our limited 
historical sources by turning to materials that do not explicitly address the queried 
concepts. Interdisciplinary knowledge can help us to glean a profound understanding of cultural ideals even in technical texts, in which cultural ideologies are 
embedded within described practices rather than stated directly. From these 
practice-focused texts, we can extract underlying cultural ideas and decipher how 
a single issue can expose various debates and tensions well beyond it.

CHINESE ABSTRACT
舊樂新風——長孫紹遠與北周的禮樂建制
魏晉南北朝時期（220–589），在非漢族音樂文化、樂器演奏廣泛傳播與興盛發展的過程 
中，中國北方政權內部仍然延續著他們漢民族先輩的一些音樂傳統。朝臣和官員們在禮樂 
實踐中援引經典文獻展開討論，同時加入他們自己的創新性理解。本文聚焦北周王朝 
（557–581）新立之際的官員長孫紹遠（506–565）與當時被俘的南朝梁國官員裴正（卒 
於590）之間一段激烈的交鋒，他們就王朝禮樂演奏中懸掛的甬鐘的數量與排列進行了辯 
論。本文認為，這些辯論遠遠超過了表面議題，而是反映學者們利用音樂理論推動構建其 
所認可的政治意識形態。就此文本而言，討論圍繞周禮禮樂的闡釋模型與漢代呂氏春秋已 
有音樂模型的對照，二者都深深植根於各自的宇宙觀與政治理念，特別是關於王權象徵意 
義。
